clinicalPearls: A complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy defined by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury.
Driven by dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway, most often from mutations in CFH, CFI, C3, CFB, CD46 (MCP) or thrombomodulin, or from acquired anti-factor H autoantibodies.
Distinct from typical HUS caused by Shiga toxin-producing bacteria and from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura due to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency.
The blood film shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes) with raised lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin and a negative direct antiglobulin test.
Often unmasked by a trigger such as infection, pregnancy, certain drugs or transplantation, even though the underlying defect is constitutional.
Terminal complement blockade with an anti-C5 monoclonal antibody has transformed outcomes and is the treatment of choice.
Anti-factor H antibody-mediated disease is frequently associated with homozygous deletion of CFHR1 and CFHR3 and may warrant immunosuppression alongside complement blockade.
CD46 (MCP) mutations, affecting a membrane-bound regulator, tend to carry a better prognosis and lower risk of recurrence after kidney transplantation than factor H mutations.
reference.pathophysiology: Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a thrombotic microangiopathy arising from uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway on endothelial surfaces. Under normal conditions this pathway is held in check by regulatory proteins including factor H, factor I and membrane cofactor protein (CD46); loss-of-function mutations in these regulators, gain-of-function mutations in the effectors C3 or factor B, or acquired autoantibodies against factor H permit unchecked formation of the C3 and C5 convertases and deposition of the terminal membrane attack complex on microvascular endothelium, particularly in the kidney. The resulting endothelial injury exposes prothrombotic surfaces, triggering platelet activation and microthrombus formation within the microcirculation. Red cells are mechanically fragmented as they pass through these partially occluded vessels, producing microangiopathic haemolysis with schistocytes, while platelets are consumed, causing thrombocytopenia, and renal microvascular thrombosis manifests as acute kidney injury. A genetic or acquired complement abnormality is commonly present but frequently requires an environmental trigger such as infection, pregnancy, drugs or transplantation to precipitate an overt episode, which explains the incomplete penetrance seen within affected families.
additionalDifferentials: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura from severe ADAMTS13 deficiency
Secondary thrombotic microangiopathy from malignant hypertension, pregnancy including HELLP, autoimmune disease or malignancy
Drug-induced thrombotic microangiopathy such as with calcineurin inhibitors or certain chemotherapy
Cobalamin C defect-associated thrombotic microangiopathy in infants
additionalInvestigations: Blood film for schistocytes, with lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, reticulocytes and direct antiglobulin test
ADAMTS13 activity to exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which should not be severely deficient in aHUS
Stool culture and Shiga toxin or PCR testing to exclude STEC-associated HUS
Complement studies including C3, C4, factor H and factor I levels, factor H autoantibodies and CD46 expression on leucocytes
Genetic testing of complement regulators and effectors (CFH, CFI, CFB, C3, CD46, THBD) and CFHR gene arrangements
Renal biopsy where the diagnosis is unclear, showing thrombotic microangiopathy
Pregnancy test and a screen for secondary triggers
redFlags: The full triad of microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, requiring urgent specialist referral
Neurological involvement such as confusion or seizures, or cardiac and gastrointestinal ischaemia from extrarenal microangiopathy
Rapidly rising creatinine or oligo-anuria requiring dialysis
Recurrence of thrombotic microangiopathy in a kidney transplant
reference.prognosis: Before complement inhibition, atypical HUS frequently progressed to end-stage renal failure or death and recurred after transplantation, particularly with factor H mutations. Terminal complement blockade has markedly improved renal recovery and survival, although prognosis still varies with the underlying genetic defect and the timeliness of treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal ADAMTS13 or negative Shiga toxin result excludes a treatable microangiopathy, since aHUS is a diagnosis reached by active exclusion of mimics
Delaying complement blockade while awaiting genetic results, given that many patients have no identifiable mutation yet still respond
Proceeding to kidney transplantation without a complement risk assessment, risking early recurrence
Overlooking a precipitating trigger such as pregnancy, drugs or infection
Misclassifying secondary thrombotic microangiopathy as primary complement-mediated disease
references: International consensus guidance on atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
